question: Prinos CO2 storage project: SEIA, geological hazards and the Seveso Directive disregarded, principle of prevention at risk of violation

In its reply to my question Ε-001877/20251, the Commission failed to respond to the critical issues concerning the legality of the CO2 storage project in Prinos: — it did not answer whether the existence of a Strategic Environmental Impact Assessment (SEIA) had been checked in accordance with Directive 2001/42/EC prior to the project’s inclusion in the Connecting Europe Facility (13.

11‑EL‑W‑M‑24‑Prinos CO2), nor whether neighbouring countries received the required advance information (Article 7), despite the project’s transboundary maritime impact; — it did not answer whether it was aware of geological reports and risk assessment for the undersea storage, despite the project’s location on top of the Anatolian fault line, where there is a risk of seismic or volcanic destabilisation of geological storage formations; — it did not specify whether the start of construction works without the prior submission of complete emergency plans and safety reports (Directive 2012/18/EU – Seveso III) was compatible with the principles of EU law, in particular the principle of prevention under Article 191 TFEU.
In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.
Can it confirm whether the SEIA and the transboundary consultation were carried out in advance in line with Directive 2001/42/EC?

Has the Commission examined the geological conditions and proximity to the Anatolian fault line in order to request the suspension of the project until a full SEIA has been submitted and a transboundary consultation and geotechnical risk assessment have been carried out?

How does the Commission ensure that projects under the Connecting Europe Facility (CEF) are not carried out before the obligations under the Seveso III Directive have been fulfilled, environmental assessments carried out and the principle of prevention under Article 191 TFEU applied?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.9.2025) In its reply to question Ε-001877/2025, the Commission explained that national authorities are primarily responsible for ensuring that all obligations under EU law are met (including crossborder consultation, assessment of geological conditions, the impact of the proximity to the Anatolian fault line, etc.)

, as well as compliance with the Do No Significant Harm Technical Guidance1. However, Directive 2009/31/EC2 requires Member States to make available to the Commission the permit applications and any other material taken into consideration when deciding on the award of a CO2 storage permit.

The Commission examines these, including any environmental impact assessment, against the requirements of the Directive and issues a non-binding opinion on the draft permit within four months of receipt of the documentation. The Greek competent authority is still preparing the documentation. Once the full documentation is submitted, the Commission will complete its review and issue its opinion.

The competent authority shall notify the final decision to the Commission, and where it departs from the Commission opinion it shall state its reasons. Beneficiaries of all Connecting Europe Facility (CEF)3 grants must implement the action in compliance with all applicable EU, international and national legal obligations.

In the specific case, according to the information submitted, the project is subject to compliance with Environmental Impact Assessment Directive4. Furthermore, the Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)5 for the activities covered by the CEF Grant Agreement6 is one of the deliverables, to be completed before the start of the related works.
This will be monitored as part of the relevant reporting and monitoring obligations.
